newsitem.title: INDIA: BMW sees bright future in India but on slow road.
newsitem.headline: BMW sees bright future in India but on slow road.

text.p: German carmaker Bayerische Motoren Werke AG (BMW) sees a big future for its cars in India and the rest of Asia but plans to proceed cautiously, its chairman, Bernd Pischetsrieder, said on Tuesday.
"India will become one of the most important markets in the future but not in the next three years," Pischetsrieder told reporters in the Indian capital.
Pischetsrieder said BMW's market share in Asia was low compared with other regions, but saw big scope for its luxury cars.
"Our aim is to become the leading company in the Far East in the segment we are looking at," he said.
He said market potential was limited in India because incomes were not yet at levels suitable for BMW.
"We, as a company, clearly think we don't want to dump cars without being able to give technical support," he said. "We are clearly determined to go on the slow, sustainable growth route."
India last month approved BMW's proposal to hold 51 percent in a joint venture with India's Hero group. Other details have not been worked out yet, BMW officials said.

The officials said BMW planned to launch by the end of 1997 its 5-series 2.5 litre diesel-engine cars in India, in collaboration with the Hero group. The investment amount has not been finalised with the Indian government.
The cars, priced at around $40,000 in the United States, would be assembled in India.
Production volumes in India would not justify manufacture of most of the parts in India, Pischetsrieder said.
BMW's launch would come after an uneasy start by Daimler Benz, which launched its Mercedes cars in India last year.
Daimler Benz faced some cancellations believed to be linked to the launch of comparatively cheap models by other makers.
India's middle-class market is being wooed by Ford Motor's Escort model and General Motors' Opel Astra, and South Korean Daewoo Corp's Cielo.
These cars have smaller engines than BMW's 2.5 litre model.
Mercedes has denied a lack of demand for its models but says there was a temporary build-up of stocks. It said last month it had sold 1,500 cars in India after sales began in January.
At 2.4 million rupees ($67,225), its model in India costs roughly four times that of Daewoo's Cielo.
"We would find it difficult, too," Pischetsrieder said in reply to a question on Mercedes's position but added that BMW was prepared to look for long-term potential.
BMW is already assembling motorcycles in India in collaboration with the Hero group.
